text: READ UNCOMMITTED is the loosest isolation level there is. You set it the same way as every other level -- SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED -- and it changes what a read actually does under the hood: it stops taking shared locks for itself, and it stops honoring other sessions' locks too.
You'll also see this requested per query, with a table hint instead of a session setting -- WITH (NOLOCK) has the exact same effect, scoped to just that one query instead of the whole session.

Because it isn't taking or honoring locks at all, READ UNCOMMITTED is the only isolation level where all three classic anomalies can happen: dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads. It's not just looser than the others -- it's the single level responsible for the dirty read being possible in the first place. Every stricter level rules that one out completely.

So why would anyone use it? It trades away correctness for raw concurrency -- no blocking on reads, ever, at the cost of potentially wrong answers. That's rarely acceptable for anything touching money or inventory. Where it sometimes shows up is rough, approximate reporting against a busy table, where being off by a row for a moment genuinely doesn't matter.

Even then, there's usually a better modern answer: RCSI, which we'll cover two lessons from now. It gives you the same non-blocking reads, but without the dirty-read risk, because it reads a last-committed version of the row instead of in-flight, uncommitted data.

Next lesson, we move to SQL Server's actual default: READ COMMITTED, the level every connection runs under unless you say otherwise -- and the point where dirty reads stop being possible at all. See you there.
